food.text: Typical Iranian main dishes combine rice with meat, vegetables and nuts. Herbs such as parsley, fenugreek, chives, mint, savory and coriander are used often, both fresh and dried. Second only to rice is the production and use of wheat.

A consistent feature of Persian cuisine is the abundant use of fruit alongside meats and in rice dishes. The most commonly used fruits include plums, pomegranates, quince, prunes, apricots, barberries and raisins.

By the 20th century, modern technology and new methods of production and packaging lifted Iran's lavashak industry to a higher level. Large lavashak production companies arose in this period, and the fruit leather also became a popular food item abroad.

Lavashak is a sour and salty or sweet fruit leather made from purees of fruits such as plums, apricots or pomegranates. For generations it was prepared in the traditional way at home, and it is now also industrially manufactured.

The southern coast of the Caspian Sea, which includes the provinces of Gilan, Mazanderan, Alborz and Golestan, has a fertile environment that shapes its cooking. Kateh, a method of cooking rice, originates there. It is also eaten as breakfast, either heated with milk and jam or cold with cheese and garlic.

Polow is the Persian word for pilaf, a rice dish stuffed with cuts of vegetables, fruits and beans, usually served with chicken or red meat. Dami dishes are similar but are cooked with the dami method, all in one pot.
Caviar fish roes hail from the Caspian region of Iran. They are typically served with eggs in frittatas and omelettes, or eaten simply with lavash and butter.

Fish is commonly eaten in Gilan province, where Caspian kutum is a staple and is usually served fried along with rice. Smoked fish, called mahi doodi, is also popular and is usually steamed together with rice.

Local cookies called koluče are popular desserts in Gilan, particularly those from the region of Fuman. Another notable dessert there is reshteh khoshkar, made of fried rice flour dough filled with sugar and nuts.

art.text: The Royal Tehran Hilton opened in 1962, during the Pahlavi era, as a modern hotel tower in Tehran. It was designed by the Iranian architect Heydar Ghiai and originally held 259 rooms.
In 2020 the BBC broadcast Art of Persia, a three-part documentary series about the history and culture of Iran. It was presented by Samira Ahmed.

In recent years, major exhibitions of Persian history, culture and art abroad have chosen the name Persia. Examples include "7000 Years of Persian Art" in Vienna and Berlin, and "Persia; Thirty Centuries of Culture and Art" in Amsterdam.
tags: Persia; Thirty Centuries of Culture and Art

art.text: A second tower was added to the Tehran hotel in 1972. It contained 291 more rooms, so the hotel grew well beyond its original single tower of 259 rooms.

war.text: The Persian campaign of World War I was devastating for Persia. Over 2 million Persian civilians died, mostly due to the Persian famine of 1917-1919, which was influenced by British and Russian actions. The country was officially neutral when the fighting began in December 1914.

Beginning in December 1914, Ottoman, British and Russian forces fought across Persia even though the country was officially neutral. The fighting ended with the Armistice of Mudros on 30 October 1918. Local Persian units also fought against the Entente and Ottoman forces.

The First World War proved devastating for Persia. Over 2 million Persian civilians died in the conflict, mostly of famine in the Persian famine of 1917 to 1919, which was influenced by British and Russian actions.

The Iran-Iraq War began with the Iraqi invasion of Iran in September 1980 and lasted eight years, until a United Nations brokered ceasefire took effect in August 1988. It was fought as large-scale trench warfare, with deliberate attacks on civilians, including Iraqi chemical attacks. The first known Iraqi chemical attack probably came in 1980 near Susangerd, and Iraq's use later included mustard gas and, from 1987, attacks on Iranian civilian targets such as Sardasht. The war caused around 500,000 deaths, not counting the related Anfal campaign, making it the deadliest conventional war ever fought between regular armies of developing countries.

Sweden sent military officers to Persia from 1911 to help modernize the army and build a gendarmerie able to fight off insurgents, whose frequent raiding made the roads difficult to traverse. Persia's government wanted a neutral power, fearing British intervention. The first officers arrived under General Harald Hjalmarson in 1911. The gendarmes had several run-ins with clan members and insurgents and scored many victories, even killing a local chieftain.

At the start of World War I, the Ottomans invaded Iranian Azerbaijan. The Russians, aided by Assyrians under Agha Petros and Armenian volunteer units, clashed with them repeatedly. After the Russian Revolution of 1917 most Russian troops withdrew, and the Ottomans occupied significant portions of the country until the war ended.

In February 1921, Reza Khan, commander of the Persian Cossack Brigade, staged a coup and became the effective ruler of Iran. In 1925 he was proclaimed monarch as Reza Shah Pahlavi, establishing the last Iranian royal dynasty.

The bloodiest battles of the Swedish-led gendarmes took place at Kazerun in 1914, where several gendarmes died fighting under Josef Pousette. Pousette had earlier been injured fighting against insurgents in Tehran. The battles were bloody and Swedish officers were at serious risk in Persia, yet many still joined the gendarmes, attracted by better pay and opportunities than in Sweden.

The Swedish officers in Persia were seen as pro-German, and they fought the Allies in battles including the Battle of Qom and the Battle of Robat Karim. In 1915 Russia and Britain pressured Sweden to call the officers back, and none remained by 1916. Five Swedes stayed on as volunteers under German leadership.
Between 1914 and 1918, Ottoman troops massacred many thousands of Iran's Assyrian and Armenian population. These killings were part of the Assyrian and Armenian genocides.

On 21 January 1920, the Battle of Shekar Yazi pitted the Kurdish leader Simko Shikak against Iranian government forces, who had attacked from the mountains around Salmas and Urmia. Simko ordered Amar Khan Shikak and his cavalry, including 200 Kurdish Zibaris, to hit the positions of the Iranian commander Amir Arshad. After a heavy battle they defeated the army and killed Amir Arshad. With their commander dead, the Iranian soldiers' morale declined, and the defeat and dispersion of the Iranian forces caused a great reaction throughout Iran.

Several Swedes and Persians died in combat with the insurgents between 1914 and 1916, in conflicts such as the Battle of Bouin and the Battle of Qazvin, where the gendarmes captured 8,000 sheep. The Swedes also persecuted and captured all the clan members of Abba Khan, who was shot by Boris Möller.
The Swedish-led gendarmerie continued to have Swedish leadership until 1921. It later ceased to exist when it merged into the Shahrbani in 1992.

literature.text: In the twenty-first century, a new generation of Iranian poets continues to work in the New Poetry style. Thanks to efforts to translate their works, these poets now attract an international audience. Milad Khanmirzaei is named as one emerging young poet among them.

Samarkand, a 1988 historical novel by the French-Lebanese writer Amin Maalouf, revolves around the 11th-century Persian poet Omar Khayyám and his poetry collection, the Rubaiyat. The novel received the Prix Maison de la Presse.

Éditions Bruno Doucey published a selection of forty-eight poems by Garus Abdolmalekian, titled Our Fists under the Table, in 2012. The poems were translated into French by Farideh Rava. The book is an example of Iranian New Poetry reaching readers abroad.

In Maalouf's novel Samarkand, the first half is set in 11th-century Persia and Central Asia. It recounts the creation of Omar Khayyám's Rubaiyat, his dealings with Nizam al-Mulk and Hassan al-Sabbah, and his love affair with a female poet of the Samarkand court.

When Jordan Mechner created the Prince for the 1989 game Prince of Persia, he drew his concepts for the character from Near Eastern mythology such as One Thousand and One Nights and the Shahnameh. Persian and Near Eastern literature thus shaped a modern video game hero.

Babak Abazari (1984 to 2015) was both a poet and a publisher, and he is counted among the notable names of the newer generation of Iranian poets. He died under mysterious circumstances in January 2015.

The second half of Samarkand follows a fictional American, Benjamin Omar Lesage, who tries to obtain the fictional original copy of the Rubaiyat. He witnesses Persian history through the Persian Constitutional Revolution of 1905-1907, only to lose the manuscript in the sinking of the RMS Titanic.

Iranian writing reached beyond Iran's borders in the 20th century. Lahouti, an Iranian poet living in exile in Russia, exerted a special influence on Persian poets in Afghanistan. In the second half of the century, Iranians such as Farrokhi Yazdi and Ahmad Shamlou also shaped newly established Afghan prose and poetry.

Reviewing Samarkand for The Independent, Ahmed Rashid called it an extraordinary book that is far more than a simple historical novel. He compared it to the embroidery of an oriental carpet, weaving back and forth through the centuries and linking the poetry, philosophy and passion of the Sufi past with modernism.

Speaking in 2010, Jordan Mechner said that while writing the series bible for future Prince of Persia games, he tried to force the Prince into the conventions of western fiction. In doing so, he was forgetting the character's literary origins.

science.text: Iran's university population grew from 100,000 in 1979 to 4.7 million in 2016. This expansion came through education and training, even though international sanctions affected almost all aspects of research over roughly 30 years.

According to the Institute for Scientific Information, Iran increased its academic publishing output nearly tenfold from 1996 to 2004. It ranked first in the world for output growth rate, ahead of China, which managed a threefold increase.
Iran's share of the world's scientific output rose from 0.0003% in 1970 to 0.29% in 2003. Even after that huge improvement, its total share of global output remained small.

Thomson Reuters found that Iran increased its science and technology output fivefold from 2000 to 2008. Most of the growth was in engineering and chemistry, and by 2008 Iran accounted for 1.02% of the world's total output.
According to the UNESCO science report 2010, the Iranian government provided almost 75% of all research funding in the country. Iranian businesses contributed only about 11% of the total in 2008.
In 2008, 25% of the scientific articles Iran published were international coauthorships. The top five countries coauthoring with Iranian scientists were the US, UK, Canada, Germany and France.
Iran devoted 0.50% of GDP to research and development in 2001. Spending peaked at 0.67% in 2008 and fell to 0.33% in 2012, while the world average in 2013 was 1.7%.

Iran's government has put much of its research budget into high technologies such as nanotechnology, biotechnology, stem cell research and information technology. In 2006 it also wiped out the financial debts of all universities to ease their budget constraints.

Iran's limited research budget is being directed toward small innovative businesses, business incubators and science and technology parks. These are the types of enterprises that employ university graduates.
Iran's national science budget was about $900 million in 2005, and it had not seen any significant increase for the previous 15 years.

politics.text: In 1925, Iran's Majles, meeting as a constituent assembly, deposed the Qajar dynasty and proclaimed Reza Khan shah, founding the Pahlavi dynasty. It was the last Iranian royal dynasty. Its overthrow in 1979 ended Iran's over 2,500-year-old monarchy.

In 1935, Reza Shah asked foreign governments to use the name "Iran" rather than "Persia" in official correspondence. Until then the country had been known in the Western world as the Imperial State of Persia.

By 1978 the Shah was wildly unpopular, and when hundreds of thousands of protesters kept demonstrating despite martial law, security forces opened fire on the crowds in the incident known as Black Friday. The Iranian Revolution in 1979 overthrew the monarchy, and the Shah fled. When Ruhollah Khomeini returned from exile, violence broke out between his supporters and the interim government of Shapour Bakhtiar, and Bakhtiar fled Iran in disguise. The Islamic Republic of Iran was then established, and Khomeini became its first supreme leader in December 1979.

Secularist efforts ultimately succeeded under the Pahlavi dynasty, which ruled from 1925 to 1979. The 1953 coup, orchestrated by Western powers, created a backlash in Iran and was among the causes of the Iranian Revolution.

In February 1921, Reza Khan, commander of the Persian Cossack Brigade, led a coup d'etat against the Qajar government, becoming the effective ruler of Iran. He was later proclaimed monarch as Reza Shah Pahlavi, reigning from 1925 to 1941.

In 1919, British Foreign Secretary Lord Curzon issued the Anglo-Persian Agreement to the Persian government. It guaranteed British access to Iranian oil fields and gave drilling rights to the Anglo-Persian Oil Company. The British government also attempted to establish a protectorate over Iran.

The Persian Constitutional Revolution sought to establish a Western-oriented, democratic civil society with an elected parliament, the Majles, a relatively free press and other reforms. Russia intervened to support the Shah and abolish the constitution: the Cossacks bombarded the Majilis in June 1908 and occupied Tehran, and more Russian army brigades occupied Tabriz after April 1909. The constitutionalists retook the capital in July 1909, but after Britain and Russia forced Shuster out of Iran with a 1911 ultimatum that the Majles unanimously rejected, the Russian army invaded the capital again and suspended the parliament. The Tsar ordered his troops in Tabriz "to act harshly and quickly", and purges led to many executions of prominent revolutionaries, which the British ambassador George Head Barclay reportedly disapproved of as a "reign of terror".

On 25 August 1941 the British and Soviets launched a surprise invasion of Iran, after Reza Shah refused to expel the Germans living there. Iran had declared neutrality in World War II, but its government surrendered after less than a week of fighting and the country was occupied. Reza Shah was forced to abdicate in favor of his 21-year-old son, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, and died in exile in South Africa on 26 July 1944, aged 66.

In 2003, Shirin Ebadi, Iran's first female judge during the Pahlavi era, won the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts in promoting human rights. In 1996, 14 women had been elected to the Islamic Consultative Assembly.
Ahmad Shah Qajar went into exile in Europe in 1923. In October 1925, Reza Khan induced the Majles to depose him and to exclude the Qajar dynasty permanently.

By June 1914, Russia had established near-total control over its northern zone of Iran. Britain had gained influence over Baluch and Bakhtiari tribal leaders in the southeastern zone. This Anglo-Russian partition weakened Qajar Iran before the First World War.

In November 1971, Iranian forces seized control of three uninhabited but strategic islands at the mouth of the Persian Gulf: Abu Musa and the Tunb islands. This came during a period when Mohammad Reza Pahlavi was modernising the armed forces and Iran protected its interests militarily in the region.

A survey report titled Iranian Public Opinion After the Protests found that 74.2% support prosecution in some form for protestors chanting against Islam or religious laws. 42.3% support prosecution without harsh punishment and 31.9% favor harsh punishment, while only 19.9% say most should be released. For protestors chanting against government policies, only 30.7% support prosecution and just 3.7% favor harsh punishment, and 64.5% say most should be released.
tags: Iranian Public Opinion After the Protests

politics.text: Surveys between July 2014 and January 2018 asked whether policymakers should take religious teachings into account. Those answering "A lot" ranged from 44% in July 2014 to 47.2% in January 2018, so a majority consistently favored at least some role for religion.
Only one grand ayatollah besides Khomeini, Hussein-Ali Montazeri, approved of the velayat-e faqih concept at the time of the revolution. Montazeri later disavowed it entirely in 1988.

The 1921 coup was assisted by the British government, which wished to halt Bolshevik penetration of Iran because of the threat to British India. Yet Reza Shah later fought and deposed British-backed figures such as Sheikh Khazal, contradicting claims that he was a British puppet. He also curtailed the Majlis, effectively turning it into a rubber stamp.

philosophy.text: Khosrow Bagheri has said that one main part of philosophical work in Iran today is local philosophy dominated by the school of Mulla Sadra. That school combines mysticism, philosophy and Islamic religious views, in line with an old metaphysical inclination.

Iran has a relatively strong translation movement that gives readers important sources of contemporary philosophy in Persian. Analytic authors such as Wittgenstein, Searle and Kripke appear alongside continental thinkers such as Nietzsche, Heidegger and Foucault.

Ahmad Fardid was a prominent Iranian philosopher and professor at Tehran University who was deeply influenced by the German thinker Martin Heidegger. He considered Heidegger the only philosopher whose insights matched the principles of the Islamic Republic.

Fardid coined the concept of "Westoxication", which Jalal Al-e-Ahmad later popularized in his widely known book Gharbzadegi. After the Iranian Revolution of 1979, the idea became one of the core ideological teachings of Iran's new Islamic government.

Abdolkarim Soroush, a former philosophy professor at the University of Tehran, became one of the most influential figures in Iran's progressive religious intellectual movement. His ideas, founded on relativism, led supporters and critics to compare his role in reforming Islam to that of Martin Luther in reforming Christianity.

Khomeini's lectures on the Guardianship of the Jurist were compiled into the book Islamic Government, first published in 1970. It argued that a leading Islamic jurist must provide political guardianship over the people and nation, and a modified form of the doctrine entered the 1979 Constitution of the Islamic Republic.

Seyyed Hossein Nasr returned to Iran in 1958 and became a professor of philosophy and Islamic sciences at Tehran University. At the request of Empress Farah Pahlavi he established the Imperial Iranian Academy of Philosophy, which soon became one of the most prominent centers of philosophical activity in the Islamic world.

Fardid wrote very little, so he became known as an "oral philosopher". He blamed the poverty and contamination of language, in a Heideggerian sense, though some suspect his reticence came from paralyzing perfectionism.

Soroush introduced his own definition of "religious democracy", meaning that the values of religion play a role in the public arena of a society populated by religious people. The subject became one of intense research in Iranian intellectual circles.

Muhammad Husayn Tabataba'i held study sessions in his home in Qom that critiqued the philosophical foundations of communism. They produced The Principles of Philosophy and the Method of Realism, published in 1953 with footnotes by Murtaza Mutahhari.
tags: Principles of Philosophy and the Method of Realism

philosophy.text: Tabataba'i produced Tafsir al-Mizan, a twenty-seven-volume work of Quranic exegesis, between 1954 and 1972. He is considered one of the most prominent thinkers of modern Shia Islam, and Allameh Tabataba'i University in Tehran is named after him.

Bagheri notes that Iranian philosophers have also concentrated on a local polar contrast between Popper and Heidegger. Because of the religious atmosphere, they have also focused on the philosophy of religion.

Fardid decried the anthropocentrism and rationalism that classical Greece brought, which he said replaced the authority of God and faith with human reason. He even criticized Islamic philosophers such as al-Farabi and Mulla Sadra for having absorbed Greek philosophy.

Morteza Motahhari taught philosophy at the University of Tehran for 22 years. He emphasized teaching over writing, so after his death his students turned his lectures into books, and Sadra Publication had issued more than sixty volumes by mid-2008.

culture.text: Historically, Iran was commonly called "Persia" in the Western world. In 1935, during an international gathering for Nowruz, Reza Shah Pahlavi officially asked foreign delegates to use the name "Iran" in formal correspondence. "Iran" and "Iranian" then became the standard terms for the country and its citizens.

Iranian cinema won worldwide attention after the Cultural Revolution. Abbas Kiarostami put Iran firmly on the map of world cinema when he won the Palme d'Or for Taste of Cherry in 1997. Iranian films have since appeared at prestigious festivals such as Cannes, Venice and Berlin.

Iran has been governed as an Islamic republic since the Revolution of 1979. It is based on the doctrine of Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist (velayat-e faqih). Shia Islam and the Ja'fari school are the official religion and the basis of the legal system.

In 1959, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi approved a committee's recommendation to reverse the 1935 name decision. The committee was led by the scholar Ehsan Yarshater, after concerns that the native name had, in Mohammad Ali Foroughi's words, "turned a known into an unknown". The result was that Persia and Iran could be used interchangeably.
Asghar Farhadi has received a Golden Globe Award and two Academy Awards. He represented Iran for Best Foreign Language Film in 2012 and 2017 with A Separation and The Salesman.

Since the 1979 Revolution, Iranian women have lost nearly all the rights they had gained in 1962 under Mohammad Reza Pahlavi. Restrictions imposed since then include mandatory Hijab. By law, a woman's testimony in court is worth half that of a man's, the age of consent for women is 9, and marital rape is legal. Women cannot leave the country without the formal permission of their guardians (father or husband), and they cannot run for president or become a judge. Even so, large numbers of women entered civil service and higher education after the revolution.

Some traditional Iranian games were demonstrated at the 1974 Asian Games, which Iran hosted. It was a way of showing that traditional Persian culture could coexist with modern Western culture. Many such games have since started to disappear due to urbanisation, computer games, and neglect by cultural institutions.

In the 2011 Iranian census, 99.38% of Iranians identified as Muslim. A 2024 Gallup report found that 72% of respondents in Iran said they were religious, 27% said they were not, and 1% said they were atheist.

During the Pahlavi era, the Royal Tehran Hilton hosted famous guests, including Ethiopian Emperor Haile Selassie and King Hussein of Jordan. The Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins also stayed there.

In 2020, Ashkan Rahgozar's "The Last Fiction" became the first representative of Iranian animated cinema in the competition section at the Academy Awards. It competed in the Best Animated Feature and Best Picture categories.
Of Iran's Muslim population, 90-95% are Shia and 5-10% are Sunni. In 2024, U.S. News & World Report placed Iran 3rd on its ranking of the most religious nations.

After the Iranian revolution in 1979 severed all foreign hotel management contracts, the Royal Tehran Hilton was renamed the Esteghlal Hotel, meaning "Independence" in Persian. Today it belongs to the state-run Parsian International Hotels Co., and a third tower is under construction.

A 2009 Gallup poll showed that 83% of Iranians said religion is an important part of their daily life. A 2020 online survey by GAMAAN found that 8.8% of Iranians surveyed self-identified as atheists. A July 2023 survey found 7% identified as atheists and 16% as humanist, an option offered for the first time.
